title: Naso: the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
hookLine: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee", still said over children and congregations
tomorrow: Naso: the same gift twelve times (Numbers 7)

cards: Friday night, in a lot of Jewish homes, before the meal. A parent puts both hands on a child's head. The child might be four and wriggling, seventeen and rolling their eyes, or thirty and home for the weekend.

The parent says a few quiet words, the same every week. In a synagogue in Jerusalem, every morning, a row of men with prayer shawls over their heads lift their hands toward the congregation and chant those very words.
They come from today's portion, and they're three lines long.

teach.b: God tells Moses to give Aaron and his sons these words for blessing the people.
"The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."
In Hebrew it's Birkat Kohanim, the blessing of the priests.
Count the Hebrew words and they grow: three, then five, then seven, like a breath getting deeper. The first line asks for blessing and protection, the things that keep a life safe.
The second asks for God's face to shine: warmth, favor, grace. The third asks God to lift up a face toward you, the same root as naso, lift, and ends with shalom, peace.
Right after, the Torah adds that the priests shall put God's name upon the people, and God will bless them.

The priests speak, but it is God who blesses. The kohanim are a channel, not the source. Descendants of Aaron, kohanim, still say it today: every day in Israel, and on festivals in many synagogues outside Israel.

They raise their hands with fingers spread, prayer shawls over their heads, and the congregation lowers its eyes. At home on Friday night, parents say it over their children. The words are old outside the Bible, too.
In 1979, archaeologists near Jerusalem found two tiny silver scrolls, rolled up like amulets, centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls.

teach.h: THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.
teach.b: Inscribed on them: a version of this blessing.

how: Kohanim, descendants of Aaron, chant the priestly blessing with raised hands in synagogue: daily in the Land of Israel and in many Sephardic communities, on festivals in many Ashkenazi communities elsewhere. Many parents say it over their children on Friday night.

place them on each person's head.

practice: Bring one person to mind, a child, a friend, a parent, someone far away or struggling, and picture their face.
If these words fit your life, say the three lines silently toward them, one line per breath, letting each grow a little longer the way the Hebrew does.
If they don't, simply hold the person in mind and wish them safety, warmth and peace.
